'''Carlos Graef Fernández''' (February 25, 1911 – January 13, 1988) was a Mexican physicist and mathematician. A graduate of the [[National Autonomous University of Mexico]] (UNAM) and the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), he was a founding member of the Mexican Mathematical Society and the [[Mexican Physical Society]]. He helped to establish the [[Tonantzintla Observatory]] and he later directed it. He received the [[National Prize for Arts and Sciences (Mexico)|National Prize for Arts and Sciences]] in 1970.

==Biography==
Graef Fernández was born in [[Guanaceví|Guanaceví, Durango]], where his father was a [[mining engineer]]. He had two younger siblings; his brother Hermann became an accomplished physician.<ref name=CGF/> He attributed an early interest in science to a physics book that his mother gave him as a child.<ref name=Garza/>

Graef Fernández first studied at a German school in Mexico, then went to Technische Hochschule Darmstadt (today [[Technische Universität Darmstadt]])<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/carlos-graef-fernandez/|title=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation {{!}} Carlos Graef Fernández|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-16}}</ref> in the German city of [[Darmstadt]] for a couple of years before returning to Mexico.<ref name="CGF">{{cite web|title=Carlos Graef Fernández|url=http://www.matmor.unam.mx/~muciray/smm/60/carlos.html|website=www.matmor.unam.mx|accessdate=December 14, 2016|language=Spanish}}</ref> He completed his undergraduate education at UNAM, and he was influenced by UNAM scientists [[Manuel Sandoval Vallarta]] and Sotero Prieto, who each mentored several successful Mexican scientists.<ref name=CGF/><ref name="Genesis">{{cite web|title=Génesis de la Facultad de Ciencias, UNAM, México|url=http://www.fciencias.unam.mx/nosotros/historia/Index|website=www.fciencias.unam.mx|accessdate=December 14, 2016|language=Spanish|archive-date=November 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161119200601/http://www.fciencias.unam.mx/nosotros/historia/Index|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] and other assistance, including a stipend awarded by Mexican president [[Lázaro Cárdenas]], Graef Fernández went to MIT.<ref name=Garza/> Around that time, he married Alicia Sánchez Castell and they later had three children. He completed a doctorate at MIT in 1940 and worked at [[Harvard University]].<ref name=CGF/>  At Harvard, Graef Fernández met [[Luis Enrique Erro]], who invited him to join the effort to found the Tonantzintla Observatory in the Mexican state of [[Puebla]].<ref name="JJS">{{cite book|last1=Saldaña|first1=Juan José|title=Science in Latin America: A History|date=2009|publisher=[[University of Texas Press]]|isbn=9780292774759|page=248|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4FLaZzmP6RIC&pg=PA248|language=en}}</ref> In ''The Skin of the Sky'', Graef Fernández is described as "small, round and prone to a cordiality that made him lovable"; he seemed an unlikely partner for Erro, who was a slender, elegant man with a hearing aid.<ref name="Skin">{{cite book|last1=Poniatowska|first1=Elena|last2=Heikkinen|first2=Deanna|title=The Skin of the Sky|date=2006|publisher=[[University of New Mexico Press]]|isbn=9780826341204|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Jd8qGjdPqCgC&pg=PA126|language=en}}</ref>

Ultimately, Graef Fernández was more interested in studying gravitational issues than astrophysics, so he sought an academic position. He joined the UNAM faculty, where he directed the Institute of Physics and the Faculty of Sciences.<ref name=Genesis/> Graef Fernández organized the meeting that led to the establishment of the Mexican Mathematical Society in 1943.<ref name="SMM">{{cite web|title=Quienes somos|url=http://www.smm.org.mx/quienes-somos.php|website=www.smm.org.mx|publisher=Mexican Mathematical Society|language=Spanish|accessdate=December 14, 2016}}</ref> He was also a founding member of the Mexican Physical Society in 1951.<ref name="FIP">{{cite web|title=Forum on International Physics: The Mexican Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/units/fip/newsletters/200906/rodriguez.cfm|website=www.aps.org|accessdate=December 13, 2016}}</ref> The society awards the Carlos Graef Fernández Prize.<ref name="Premio">{{cite web|title=Premio Carlos Graef Fernández|url=http://www.smf.mx/premio-carlos-graef-fernandez/|website=www.smf.mx|accessdate=December 13, 2016|language=Spanish|archive-date=December 20, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220113903/http://www.smf.mx/premio-carlos-graef-fernandez/|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was awarded the National Prize for Arts and Sciences in 1970.<ref name=CGF/>

Graef Fernández served on numerous committees related to the [[nuclear industry]].<ref name="ICG">{{cite web|title=Dr. Carlos Graef Fernández|url=http://abaco.izt.uam.mx/institutograef/DOCUMENTOS/biografia.pdf|publisher=Instituto Carlos Graef|language=Spanish|accessdate=December 14, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170518224106/http://abaco.izt.uam.mx/institutograef/DOCUMENTOS/biografia.pdf|archive-date=May 18, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> He was made an emeritus professor at UNAM in 1974 and died in 1988.<ref name="Garza">{{cite journal|last1=Piña Garza|first1=Eduardo|title=Carlos Graef Fernández|journal=Elementos|date=1992|issue=16|pages=41–43|url=http://www.elementos.buap.mx/num16/pdf/41.pdf|language=Spanish|access-date=2016-12-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220135636/http://www.elementos.buap.mx/num16/pdf/41.pdf|archive-date=2016-12-20|url-status=dead}}</ref>
